This study examines the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks trained via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the MNIST dataset. Leveraging recent progress in the theoretical analysis of Schrödinger operators, we demonstrate that the network's ground state resides within a spectral Barron space characterized by an adaptability to the data distribution. This finding enables the derivation of explicit rates for the bias and variance of the generalization error, which align closely with empirical results from MNIST training.

The rising popularity of brain-on-organ-on-a-chip technologies is driven by their capacity to integrate multiple tissue types, yet current research remains limited regarding multi-tissue configurations. This study introduces a novel framework utilizing the CLEVER multi-chip system to emulate a complex living environment containing a cerebral network, a vascular network, and a peripheral network. We leverage the *C. elegans* organism as a model, capitalizing on its comprehensive structural and biological documentation to facilitate effective modelling and simulation. The reported methodology employs established behavioral and anatomical data to define specific testing protocols, which are designed to assess the reliability of the multi-organ chip. By combining this multi-organ approach with *C. elegans*, this research establishes a novel pathway for mechanistic investigation and the design of future brain-organ chip architectures.

We examine a random permutation permutation $\sigma$ drawn from the uniform distribution on the set of all permutations of length $n$, denoted $\Pi_n$. This structure is organized into a decomposition tree where nodes correspond to substructures defined by the largest element within them. A substructure is classified as left-leaning if it contains more elements to the left than the right; otherwise, it is right-leaning. We recursively trace the longest path from the root down to a leaf, moving exclusively through these left-leaning or right-leaning configurations. Our findings demonstrate that as $n$ grows without limit, the length of this trajectory follows a Poisson-Dirichlet distribution with parameter $\alpha=1/2$ in the convergence limit.

A group-subgroup pair (G,H) constitutes a strong Gelfand pair whenever every irreducible character of the subgroup H induces a multiplicity-free representation on G. This paper addresses the classification of such pairs for SL(2, p), where p denotes an odd prime, addressing cases where SL(2, p) is viewed either as it stands or as part of a triple isomorphic structure.

This work investigates the central covers $\widetilde{G}$ associated with the finite general linear groups $GL(n,q)$ and their Sylow $p$-subgroups, where $p$ denotes the characteristic of the finite field, and extends the analysis to a $p$-group sharing the same central structure as the group in $GL(n,q)$. We demonstrate that the characters of central covers corresponding to the relevant Sylow $p$-subgroups are linearly dependent. Additionally, we identify the character sets for $\widetilde{Sylp}^*(GL(n,q))$—the collection of characters arising from sections of $\widetilde{G}$ involving a Sylow $p$-subgroup. We also establish the linear dependence among Gelfand--Graev modules for $\widetilde{F}GL(n,q)$ across all finite fields $ \text{GL}(n,q)$, where $ \text{GL}(n,q)$ represents a finite group of Lie type.

The SiD detector, a next-generation instrument at SLAC's Linear Collider, is engineered to precisely measure the properties of newly discovered particles, including dark matter candidates. Its outstanding momentum resolution and mass resolution stem from specific design choices: a thin, silicon-based vertex layer, an extremely precise, straw-tube-based main tracker, and the capability for particle identification across a vast energy spectrum via its electromagnetic and hadronic calorimeters. This document outlines the current status of the SiD, with a specific focus on its tracking system.

The structure of different types of ice is fundamentally linked to the behavior of its hydrogen atoms. This study investigates a newly developed local order metric (LOM) that quantifies the degree of crystalline structure around any specific site. We demonstrate that LOM values derived from simulations of amorphous water and various thermodynamic ice phases exhibit similar behavior, suggesting a degree of universality. Furthermore, LOM results align closely with conventional measures of order parameters. We also examine the effects of temperature and pressure on LO M across amorphous water and multiple ice phases. Finally, we analyze the connection between LO M and the melting process within amorphous water.

This study introduces a straightforward and cost-effective method for characterizing the lattice structure of Highly Oriented Pyrolytic Graphite (HOPG) using a standard red laser pointer alongside a simple optical bench. By recording X-ray diffraction patterns and analyzing the resulting data, we determined the sample's lattice constant to be 0.2457 ± 0.0002 nm. This result is accurate to within 1.7\% relative error compared to the standard literature value of 0.2433 nm. Furthermore, the experimental setup successfully identified the presence of surface contaminants. Ultimately, this approach offers a student-friendly alternative to complex equipment for diffraction studies.

Over the last ten years, the Lean community has accumulated a substantial archive of formalized materials spanning mathematics, computer science, and engineering. This body of work serves as an invaluable resource, offering both practical examples and deep insights for those seeking to master proof construction. Nevertheless, as this collection expands, barriers to entry arise regarding accessibility and comprehension. Furthermore, the sheer volume creates significant challenges in identifying and connecting related concepts. These issues underscore the urgent need for enhanced navigation, discovery, and interpretation capabilities. Addressing these gaps aligns with Lean's mission to function as a functional library of logic and proof tactics, effectively operating as an interactive dissertation that empowers users to both learn from and contribute to a growing ecosystem of formalized knowledge.

Heliospheric oscillations, encompassing fluctuations in solar wind parameters and interplanetary magnetic fields, are typically analyzed by transforming raw data into Fourier spectra to examine power distribution across frequencies. This study introduces "audification"—a method where oscillatory data is mapped to an audible frequency range—as a complementary approach. We demonstrate through case studies of simultaneous solar wind and magnetic field measurements that audification offers a distinct advantage: it effectively isolates and highlights specific temporal periods exhibiting identical or near-identical oscillatory phases in both data sets. Furthermore, audification facilitates the straightforward visualization of phase shifts between different intervals. While the techniques yield consistent results, audification's capacity to isolate common modes across disparate plasma fields makes it a particularly valuable tool for comparative analysis.

This research investigates the thermal and dynamical stability of rotating charged black branes within a framework of string-inspired gravity, which incorporates a non-minimal dilaton-brane interaction term. Solutions to the field equations are derived for both static and dynamic configurations, allowing the analysis of their physical properties through the lens of thermodynamics. Specifically, the study examines Brane world scenarios featuring exponential and inverse scale factor laws. Numerical analyses of brane dynamics reveal that thermal stability is governed by the $\alpha$ coupling constant, with the fully back-reacted system exhibiting a distinct phase transition at a critical value of $\alpha \approx 0.75$. Furthermore, the investigation into dynamic stability via perturbation methods indicates that this critical coupling threshold is independent of temporal parameters.

Advancements in artificial intelligence have yielded significant progress in the field of natural language processing. However, despite the remarkable achievements of deep learning models, the lack of a memory-based representation for text has hindered progress, preventing systems from effectively emulating human cognitive capabilities. To address this, we introduce MEMA—a memory-enhanced text representation designed to reflect the human memory system. By integrating MEMA, we achieve a substantial improvement in text similarity assessment and a notable enhancement in note-to-document retrieval performance. These findings validate that MEMA serves as a robust bridge between machine learning architectures and human memory, enabling text processing systems to leverage memory-based representations for improved effectiveness.

We introduce a novel, physically rigorous model designed to simulate the emission spectra of young stellar objects (YSOs) featuring ionizing photoevaporating disks. This framework is fully compatible with existing atmospheric and disk radiative transfer codes, such those used for HDAT and HDISC. We apply this methodology to model the spectra of TW Hydrae, a nearby young star known to host an extended, photoevaporated disk. The results from this approach align closely with observational data across a broad range of wavelengths, from the ultraviolet to the far infrared. Specifically, we identify that the extended disk emission is essential for accurately reproducing the observed far-UV continuum. The model attributes the broad far-UV emission to a compact, hot region near the outer disk edge, where photoevaporation is most intense. The narrow, complex far-UV spectral profile is explained by the combined effects of the hot outer disk emission and the stellar atmosphere. The far-infrared excess is linked to the warm, neutral outer disk regions, while the near-infrared data are accounted for by the combined contributions of the stellar atmosphere and the warm inner disk. The inner disk's near-infrared emission is further constrained by the presence of a CO absorption band at 2.3 $\mu$m, which serves as a diagnostic tool for estimating its temperature. The model also explores a scenario in which the CO band arises from absorption within the stellar atmosphere, a possibility that could be verified through high-resolution spectroscopy.

The introduction of Angle Regulating Transformers (ARs) into power systems introduces internal faults within the regulating range that manifest as indirect asymmetrical phase deviations at the terminal levels. This paper presents an experimental evaluation of the regulation circuit's response to three distinct internal fault types: open circuit, welded contacts, and contact bridging. The study evaluates how these faults influence the regulation current and voltage output, as well as the resulting currents and voltage patterns downstream. Based on this data, an internal fault classification methodology is proposed that distinguishes among the three fault modes by analyzing inherent phase shift variations. The findings confirm that the internal current load serves as the primary indicator for identifying such faults. Furthermore, the resulting terminal and secondary-side electrical parameters provide sufficient evidence to support the differentiation of fault types.

Multicast beamforming is essential for enhancing spectral efficiency, yet it remains a difficult challenge that becomes even more complex when channel state information (CSI) is imperfect. This study examines downlink multicast beamforming optimization for multiuser massive MIMO systems under imperfect CSI conditions. We initially establish a weighted sum rate (WSR) maximization problem subject to total power constraints, noting its non-convex nature. To address this, we first convert the WSR maximization into a fractional programming (FP) problem. Subsequently, we develop a successive cancellation algorithm to transform the issue into several convex sub-problems. Within each iteration, we utilize the matrix inversion lemma alongside alternating optimization techniques to derive a sub-optimal WSR solution. Furthermore, we address scenarios where feedback CSI suffers from specific errors. We subsequently refine the beamforming optimization by integrating the impact of these errors into the formulation.

A function $f$ is deemed near exponential if there exists a constant $C>0$ such that the inequality $0 \leq f(2x)-f(x)-f(x) \leq C$ holds for all $x>0$ (or equivalently, if $f(2x) = 2f(x) + O(1)$). This paper investigates the semigroup generated by such a function $f$ within the context of endomorphisms of the additive group of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$. The findings presented here extend and generalize previous research conducted by the same group of authors, which was previously published in *Enseign. Math.* (2018).

This research addresses the exponential stability of a specific Euler–Bernoulli beam model described as a metric graph with three arms joining at a single vertex, where each arm corresponds to a uniformly hyperbolic wave equation. The stability analysis hinges on resolving the eigenvalue problem for a coupled system of four wave equations solved via the Laplace transform. By applying Fourier-Laplace analysis, this approach yields explicit expressions for the eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors. It is demonstrated that the resulting eigenvectors are uniformly (and optimally) $H^2(\Gamma)$-bounded. Furthermore, these eigenfunctions are proven to form an orthogonal, complete basis in $L^2(\Gamma)$, leading to explicit uniform estimates of the resolvent and conclusive proof of the system's exponential stability.

We introduce a Bayesian machine learning mass model that incorporates correlations between nuclei with varying proton and neutron counts. This approach achieves a prediction accuracy of 50 keV for both even-even and odd-A nuclei, surpassing the conventional 100 keV benchmark. Additionally, our method provides uncertainties that align well with observed residual errors relative to experimental data.

We introduce a technique for measuring the dielectric loss tangent ($\tan \delta$) at cryogenic temperatures, achieving a sensitivity as high as $10^{-8}$, which rivals room temperature capabilities. The method involves monitoring the decay of electric field energy stored within a dielectric material, facilitated by microwave resonators. To maximize measurement sensitivity, we employ thin dielectric films as resonator coatings, thereby minimizing the dielectric volume and allowing for the precise characterization of bulk material properties even when sample sizes are limited. We validated this approach by determining the $\tan \delta$ of sapphire, a well-characterized dielectric standard, with results matching existing bulk data to within 30% uncertainty.

Light traversing a moving dielectric undergoes a displacement in its path, a process known as the optical drag effect, of which Fresnel-Fizeau's work is a foundational element. While the traditional explanation attributes this solely to the reduced velocity of light within the medium—accounting for only reduced velocity of light within the material—this article proposes an alternative framework. This new approach attributes the phenomenon entirely to a shift in momentum resulting from energy transfer as light passes through the dielectric. We substantiate this hypothesis by examining the optical drag effect across various scenarios involving layers of dielectric media and by contrasting it with Abbe's theory of partial light drag.

We introduce a new class of approximation schemes designed to identify parameter scenarios yielding worst-case outcomes in two-stage robust optimization models featuring binary first-stage decisions and second-stage continuous variables. These approaches adapt the standard column-and-constraint generation framework typically employed for dual-fortified robust problems. Traditional exact methods for determining parameter realizations often rely on enumerating all combinations of binary variables, a strategy that is computationally prohibitive. Consequently, researchers have turned to stochastic sampling techniques, which lack reliability as they do not guarantee optimality within fixed timeframes. In contrast, our proposed approach offers provable approximation bounds while ensuring that selected worst-case examples are valid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm effectively generates particularly insightful and challenging instances suitable for testing other solution methods.

The analysis of large-scale real estate transaction datasets offers valuable insights into property values, a subject of growing interest for researchers. However, these data streams possess inherent potential for contributing to urban mobility planning, a connection that has not yet been fully explored. This study addresses this gap by introducing a novel framework that integrates real estate valuation with urban mobility planning through a multi-objective approach. The framework utilizes real estate valuation to establish a land use model and applies Bayesian inference to a spatially constrained random walker algorithm to model traffic patterns. Furthermore, an original multi-objective optimization method is presented to evaluate the trade-offs between developer interests, government policies, and societal needs. Ultimately, this research provides a innovative, data-driven foundation for creating urban mobility plans that are more efficient and sustainable.

Pattern discovery is fundamental to data analysis, yet it remains a complex challenge. While algorithms are well-established for structured data like graphs and trees, they often fail to address datasets consisting of unstructured elements, such as images or audio. To visualize and understand the distributions within pattern collections, we introduce a new framework for displaying distributions in space, which can be customized to reveal various aspects of the underlying data. We also present an interactive data exploration tool that leverages this visualization to guide users through pattern distributions. Additionally, we have integrated this approach into the SciKitPy platform to offer a user-friendly interface for data analysis and visualization.

Recent research highlights the potential of using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for learning representations from structured data. Additionally, transfer learning has emerged as a cost-effective strategy for acquiring high-quality features, particularly in machine learning tasks where target data is scarce. This study investigates a form of domain-specific transfer learning within GNNs by introducing Graph Field Transfer (GFT), a method that domain-specifically adapts GNN architectures. GFT leverages GNNs pre-trained on general graphs to initialize their parameters, subsequently fine-tuning them for downstream applications. This approach offers two main advantages: it accelerates convergence and improves final model performance. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that GFT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving substantial gains in both classification and link prediction metrics.

This paper introduces a collaborative filtering recommender system that predicts user preferences by analyzing patterns within user-item interactions, specifically utilizing items a current user has already engaged with to anticipate those they will likely choose next. The study focuses on the MovieLens 1M dataset, where each instance represents a user-film interaction. The core methodology involves treating these ratings as regression targets for a supervised learning problem, solved here through a linear model implementation via a Grid Search optimization technique. The model's performance is evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and Pearson Correlation Coefficient metrics. The experimental setup utilizes data augmentation, expanding the original dataset fivefold by generating synthetic ratings to improve model robustness. The results indicate that this approach achieves a test set RMSE of 0.8585 and a Pearson Correlation Coefficient of 0.4477.

This research introduces an on-chip multi-grating apparatus designed to direct and confine single Rubidium atoms via a single-beam optical lever. An integrated waveguide directs 780 nm laser light toward an optical trap positioned approximately 12 μm above the chip surface. When incident light is focused by this structure, the resulting optical diameter measures roughly 3 μm. The system leverages the optical lever effect to establish a deep potential depth of 1.5 k$_{\text{B}}$K, directing atoms toward the grating-induced focal point. Utilizing atom-chip technology, an 87Rb atom chip is fabricated with a specific on-chip waveguide to load a single atom. Experimental results confirm the generation of the optical trap and demonstrate the successful transfer of a solitary atom from the waveguide into the deep optical trap.

The nonlinear Hall effect arises from the nonlinear dynamics of Bloch electrons within time-periodic driving fields. This phenomenon stems from the interference of different paths taken by accelerating electrons in a band, a process governed by the nonlinear acceleration itself. The effect is fundamentally rooted in the geometric properties of the electronic wavefunctions, manifesting as a nontrivial force derived from the nonlinearity of the vector potential. Unlike the ordinary nonlinear Hall effect, which relies on broken crystal symmetry, this variant operates in systems with preserved symmetry. It was first identified in the context of the nonlinear quantum Hall effect, where it appears as the third harmonic response in systems exhibiting a nonzero Berry curvature dipole. Subsequent research has highlighted its distinct characteristics, including the effect's third harmonic response in nonlinear systems and its presence even when crystal symmetry remains intact. This discussion provides a comprehensive overview of the underlying principles, theoretical frameworks, and experimental observations associated with this phenomenon.

This study introduces a direct collocation method to solve continuous-time dynamic optimization problems, specifically the Optimal Path Planning (OPP) problem, when analytical solutions are unavailable. The system's dynamic models are numerically integrated using the Runge-Kutta 4th-order technique. To ensure a robust numerical solution, the paper examines various numbers of collocation points and polynomial orders. Furthermore, different objective function forms are evaluated to assess their influence on solution accuracy and computational efficiency. Results indicate that a solution with high numerical accuracy can be achieved through numerical integration combined with either 100 collocation points or a combination of 50 points with a 7th-order integration scheme. Finally, the paper illustrates the application of this methodology to both linear and nonlinear OPP scenarios.

A rational function $f$ defined on the Riemann sphere is termed bicritical precisely if it possesses two critical points other than its attracting basins' centers (note: the original implies exactly two critical points total, making them bicritical). The dynamics of $f$ can be described through a pair of polynomials $q_1$ and $q_2$ such that the composition $f \circ q_1 = q_2$. This relationship is referred to as the quadratic representation of $f$. The primary objective of our paper is to demonstrate that every bicritical rational map admits such a quadratic representation.

Transition metal dichalcogenides (e.g., WS$_2$) represent a promising class of two-dimensional (2D) semiconducting materials. To enable the design of novel WS$_2$-based 2D semiconducting devices, it is essential to understand their electronic properties, such as band gap and carrier mobility. This study employs a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) approach to calculate these specific properties for WS$_2$ in various configurations, including monolayer, bilayer, trilayer, bulk, and various defect scenarios. Furthermore, we examine how carrier mobility varies with different doping concentrations.

Delta lenses facilitate the declarative design of bidirectional transformations between pairs of models, yet they struggle to handle unlimited forward or backward modifications in learned models. This paper introduces an approach to exploit the similarities found in delta lenses while successfully managing these infinite sequences of changes.

This paper estimates oscillatory integrals of the form $I(\lambda)=\int_{\mathbb R^n} e^{i\lambda\phi(x)}f(x)\,dx$ when the phase function $\phi$ is real-valued, smooth, and has a non-degenerate Hessian at the origin, with $f$ being a bounded, compactly supported function. By applying wave packet decomposition, we obtain enhanced estimates for the $L^p$ norms of $I(\lambda)$ that surpass earlier work by Bourgain, Demeter, and Guo. Furthermore, these results yield new bounds for discrete oscillatory sums.

This work examines the asymptotic behavior of solutions to the Boltzmann equation near the transition from rarefied to continuum regimes, specifically analyzing how to recover a steady-state solution by perturbing from a Maxwellian distribution. While the time-evolution solution in the rarefied limit converges to the Navier-Stokes equations, recovering this continuum solution in a regime where Navier-Stokes equations no longer apply remains a significant challenge. Consequently, an alternative method is proposed to derive steady-state states that are only weakly dispersed from equilibrium. The error between exact solutions and these approximations is rigorously quantified, and their performance is benchmarked against existing computational methods. Additionally, the efficacy of a recently developed machine learning approach for capturing steady-state solutions is evaluated.

CMS presents updated results on the July 4th 2012 discovery of a Higgs-like Boson at CERN using data from the Large Hadron Collider's 7 TeV and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions. The analysis covers decays into photon pairs, tau-lepton pairs, and bottom-antiquark pairs. On December 13, 2015, CMS released a combined analysis of these three channels, which identified a significant excess around an 8 TeV mass. This measurement yielded a statistical significance of 3.9 standard deviations, with a mass of 125 GeV. The study further examined how the production cross-section multiplied by branching fractions for decays into four leptons, eight tau-leptons, and ten b-quarks varied with energy. The findings show a strong consistency with Standard Model Higgs predictions, leading to the determination of the Higgs mass at 125 GeV.

The authors outline the p-divisibility rule governing the Fourier coefficients of Siegel modular functions, which they state expands upon Wintonius' findings related to the p-divisibility characteristics of Ramanujan's tau function for Fourier coefficients.

Consequently, within topological spaces, fibration theory functions as a sub-branch of the broader framework governed by Galois theory.

When fermionic atoms are cooled to a temperature approaching absolute zero, they occupy the ground state as a collective entity known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, a state governed by the Pauli exclusion principle. This phenomenon is a direct result of fermionic nature, where no two fermions can occupy the same quantum state. In this study, we examine the collective excitation modes of a fermionic gas trapped in a harmonic potential, utilizing Bessel-Gauss-Laguerre modes as the basis set. Our analysis reveals that the energy spectrum of Bessel-Gauss-Laguerre modes aligns perfectly with the harmonic trap levels, thereby allowing us to achieve BEC at specific quantum states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the hyperparameters of the basis functions can be tuned to significantly reduce numerical errors in calculations. The approach relies on identifying and exploiting the presence of an optimal solution that strictly adheres to weight or budget constraints without any approximation. Consequently, the proposed reduction from the discrete to the continuous domain enables the derivation of the best current approximation ratios for both SUKP and BMCP through the application of continuous knapsack strategies.

We further developed a novel loss function to facilitate model optimization within this framework. Evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CSC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in spatiotemporal predictive learning tasks.

This paper examines the memory management strategies employed in functional languages, contrasting them with traditional imperative approaches. It highlights the shift from imperative-style manual pointerto-based systems, which manage memory explicitly, toward garbage collection as the standard in functional programming. The text further explores two key implementations of this concept: the Haskells runtime environment and the dataflow architecture found in languages like Clean.

Heavy neutral leptons offer a compelling framework for explaining the cosmological baryon asymmetry, and this note outlines a search strategy for these particles at the High-Luminosity LHC within channels producing three jets and missing energy. The analysis covers scenarios where the HNLs are produced in pairs and decays result in multiple neutrinos, as well as single-HNL production followed by the emission of one or more neutrinos. This study specifically targets the specific charge-parity eigenstates, J^PC = 0^(-+) and 1^(-), which are associated with the J^PC quantum numbers of the HNLs under the stated production modes.

Permutation decoding offers a way to enhance the frame error rate (FER) of polar codes by transforming them into structurally similar codes with improved performance. This study introduces an enhanced decoder that integrates list-Viterbi or maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding with pre- and post-processing permutations. The code structure is reorganized by applying a specific permutation to the information and frozen bit positions, which is then applied to polar subchannels to balance performance against frame error rate. During decoding, the receiver compares multiple candidate permutations against the received word and selects the most probable one. Simulation results confirm that this approach achieves lower FER compared to standard list-Viterbi or MAP decoding while maintaining significantly lower computational complexity.

We establish that a linear combination of data produces a well-defined point-spread function (PSF) and a consistent photometric zero-point only if the operation commutes with convolution and yields a coaddition that is commutative, associative, and idempotent. Consequently, standard nonlinearity constraints such as rounding, clipping, or clamping—often employed to eliminate extreme outliers—prevent the derivation of a defined PSF for the resulting coadded image. We propose an alternative linear coaddition method based on Hessian-filtered robust estimators, which successfully defines the PSF and remains effective in suppressing outliers.

This study presents a thermodynamic framework designed to analyze the fracture toughness of brittle and ductile crystalline solids. The proposed model relies on the concept of crack surface energy, which accounts for the energetic benefits derived from dislocation activity within the crack tip region. Within this framework, dislocations are introduced as the fundamental mechanism responsible for the fracture toughness observed in crystalline solids. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated by applying it to the fracture of ionic crystals, demonstrating its ability to accurately replicate experimental data across a range of temperatures and loading rates. Additionally, the model offers new insights into the mechanisms driving ductile fracture in crystalline solids.

The task of quantum verification asks how to compel an untrusted quantum processor to execute a specific circuit while ensuring a small, limited verifier can efficiently confirm the results. Although various interactive protocols exist, the most efficient known method, proposed by Fitzsimmons, Li, and Yuen in 2021, requires $O(n^2)$ classical processing time and $O(n)$ quantum memory for an input circuit with $n$ gates. This paper introduces a new protocol that matches the optimal $O(n)$ quantum memory of the previous state-of-the-art but significantly reduces the classical computational complexity to $O(n \cdot \text{poly}(\lambda))$ for a security parameter $\lambda$. Our approach builds upon the Fitzsimmons et al. framework by integrating quantum memory into an efficient commutative encryption scheme. We achieve this by adapting the scheme to a single-qubit setting using measurements and single-Pauli operations, which we term "Pauli encryption."

Blockchain technology is increasingly recognized as a robust solution for Internet of Things (IoT) security, offering data integrity, transparency, and trustworthiness. However, inherent blockchain limitations—specifically high energy consumption, slow transaction speeds, and scalability issues—render standard blockchains poorly suited for IoT applications. To address these constraints, various specialized architectures have been developed, categorized primarily as off-chain, hybrid, and self-contained solutions. This paper provides a comprehensive review of these blockchain-driven IoT frameworks, with a specific focus on their consensus mechanisms. We evaluate their performance across key metrics, including security, energy efficiency, and scalability, and conclude by identifying emerging research directions for this evolving field.

We introduce a new technique for capturing cell morphology using the level sets of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). This approach surpasses voxel-based methods, which lack the necessary precision, and polygon meshes, which often introduce excessive complexity. By leveraging a neural network, our model learns a parametric SDF that can be seamlessly extended to handle both 2D and 3D contexts with minimal adjustments. This framework offers significant advantages specifically in three dimensions: it reduces the reliance on manual feature engineering and increases scalability by accommodating a broader range of dataset sizes.

Accessing printed documents presents a significant challenge for individuals who are blind or have low vision. Although screen readers are the standard solution for non-digital materials, they struggle to handle complex document structures, such as forms, which often contain fields, buttons, and specific layouts. Consequently, these users face difficulties in navigating the content and completing tasks. To address this, we present a new architecture for document structure detection, utilizing object detection and object identification to convert document components into meaningful semantic labels. The system classifies detected elements into categories including buttons, form fields, images, and text. The proposed method demonstrates strong performance on the "Form 101" benchmark dataset.

This study introduces Pre-trained Encoder-based Language Model (PELM) (notably not LLM), which combines the contextual depth of BERT with the superior context retention of CTF. Our approach involves two key modifications: first, we replace BERT's one-way context attention with a bidirectional setup that incorporates self-attention mechanisms for enhanced learning efficiency. Second, we integrate a novel hybrid loss function that optimizes both contextual understanding and likelihood predictions. Our experiments demonstrate that PELM outperforms BERT across various tasks, including named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and semantic textual similarity. Additionally, our codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/yourusername/PELM.

We introduce a novel technique to detect and quantify stellar activity in exoplanet transit data, leveraging spectroscopic information from planetary atmospheres. This approach utilizes regions expected to show planetary signatures but influenced by stellar activity, using them as proxies for atmospheric effects. By modeling the relative contribution of stellar activity versus planet-induced spectral changes in the transit light curve, we model activity levels. We demonstrate this method's ability to reveal stellar activity during the transit of WASP-39B, specifically targeting water features at 3.7 and 2.7 $\mu$m. Our findings indicate that stellar activity significantly impacts the observation of the 3.7 $\mu$m water feature, potentially obscuring or mimicking genuine planetary signals. Consequently, this method offers a robust way to assess stellar activity impacts on exoplanet atmospheres observed via spectroscopy and provides critical insights for interpreting future observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

The governing equations for the shallow water system are derived within a rotating framework, accounting for both topographic effects and Coriolis forces. This work introduces the first direct time-domain dispersive model capable of precisely simulating diverse wave behaviors, including the full dispersion cycle and non-linear shoaling and breaking processes. While dispersion is typically negligible during the main phases of most tsunamis, it becomes critical for modeling short-wavelength phenomena such as whistling tsunamis. The proposed method utilizes a depth-integrated approach that incorporates vertical acceleration to capture vertical dispersion effects. A novel root-finding algorithm is applied to address the resulting quadratic vertical dispersion coefficient. Additionally, the model integrates vertical drag effects to account for the drag coefficient's vertical dependency. Validation against the non-dispersive shallow water equations confirms accuracy in the limit of low wave numbers.

We report the discovery of a population of HST-dark galaxies—objects undetected by prior Hubble Space Telescope surveys—identified through a deep JWST survey of the Fornax cluster. Utilizing 10-band NIRCam data combined with a single JWST NIRCam observation, we detected 11 galaxies at redshifts between $z=1.2$ and $2.2$ that exhibit no corresponding sources in earlier HST data. These galaxies are notably compact, with half-light radii of $r_{50}' \sim 0.15$ kpc, and possess stellar masses around $10^{10} M_{\odot}$ alongside star formation rates of $1-2 M_{\odot}$/yr. Our findings suggest that roughly 10% of the cluster's total star formation activity occurred in these previously hidden, compact systems. This study marks the first direct observation of a significant group of cluster galaxies invisible to prior HST observations, underscoring the transformative potential of JWST for exploring obscured and compact stellar populations.

We investigate a specific class of seven-dimensional gravity that includes added topological terms. By utilizing a simplified method, we derive an effective seven-dimensional Lagrangian and Lagrange's equations of motion. We then solve these equations to determine the properties of four-dimensional, static, and spherical symmetric black holes, as well as those of four-dimensional, spherical, and uncharged topological holonomy-free Riemannian manifolds.

The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a primary driver of global climate variability, notably influencing precipitation patterns throughout the seasons. This paper introduces a novel method for identifying El Niño events and their classification using a Univariate Discrete Wavelet Transform (UDWT) applied to the Ni\`{~}~\`{~}o3.4–Ni\`{~}~\`{~}n3.9 degree sea surface temperature data from the Extended Reanalysis 2 (ERS-2) dataset. This approach detects El Niño occurrences from 1980 to 2020 and distinguishes between the Eastern Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP) types. Our results indicate that CP El Ni\`{~}~\`{~}nOs are more strongly correlated with seasonal rainfall anomalies than their EP counterparts. Furthermore, the study identifies specific wavelet frequency bands that effectively distinguish these two types and map their characteristic teleconnection patterns.

Nonoffine deformation is a key feature of the mechanical response to stress in disordered solids, where its behavior is often evaluated using a procedure that decomposes the pair correlation function into a series of such deformations. This study introduces a novel alternative based on an energy framework, which relies on an energy criterion to define and constrain the parameters of nonoffine regions. We apply this new energy-based approach to the 2D disordered solid derived from the random close packing of spheres, as well as to a polyamorph of the $\gamma$-Al2O3 polymeric glass. Analysis reveals that while the magnitude and spatial distribution of the resulting nonoffine fields are largely consistent with those obtained from traditional methods, the current method offers a more precise and physically intuitive interpretation. Furthermore, these simulations suggest that energy-based strategies may prove superior in future applications aimed at identifying local deformation zones in molecular dynamics trajectories.

This study examines a single-population model representing interactions between organisms and toxic environmental byproducts. We focus on adults producing offspring via a Fisher-type recruitment mechanism while generating toxins that disperse through diffusion. Crucially, adults exhibit fear responses to these toxins, modulating their birth rates and migration patterns (separation) based on local toxin concentrations. To reflect the non-Markovian nature of memory within the system, we model these influences using a non-local framework. The analysis demonstrates that these non-local parameters can trigger bifurcations within the system. We establish the existence of steady-state solutions by constructing a unique solution to a Poisson problem to analyze the system's behavior at high environmental toxicity levels. Subsequently, we conduct a numerical investigation into how these non-Markovian parameters impact the population's spatial distribution.

Additionally, we prove that a variant of FLew, which incorporates non-commutativity alongside weakening, is proof-theoretically equivalent to Commutative Linear Logic with an infinite height derivation system, thereby confirming its status as a decidable substructural fragment.

Taxonomies are structured hierarchies that organize entities into nested classes. While embedding these into low-dimensional Euclidean spaces has proven useful for various natural language processing tasks, Euclidean models often fail to account for the significant structural nuances of complex, large-scale concepts. In contrast, vector representations within hyperbolic space demonstrate superior performance in capturing deep hierarchical structures. This paper introduces HyperbolicBEH (Hyperbolic Bounded Embedding of Hierarchies), a method for constructing both bounded hyperbolic embeddings of extensive taxonomies like Wikipedia and Euclidean versions of the same. Our approach leverages the metric geometry inherent in Scaled Poincaré Ball (P-Ball) to construct embeddings that remain geometrically accurate and strictly bounded. These P-Ball models effectively embed structural relationships, and when converted to Euclidean space, they preserve those relationships within reasonable bounds. Our experiments on the Wikipedia 1.0 dataset demonstrate that these methods significantly outperform existing models in capturing taxonomy structures and achieving more realistic visualizations in the transition from P-Ball to Euclidean space.

This work details the construction of an effective one-body Hamiltonian for the two-dimensional orientation of a specific dimer: a pair of aligned acetylene molecules ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$) situated in a plane. While parallel, uncharged molecules typically experience negligible interaction dipole moments (IDMs) with dipoles aligned along their intermolecular axis, these moments become substantial when molecules are arranged in an anti-parallel fashion. This behavior arises from long-range multipole interactions, specifically dipole-dipole ($\mu\text{-}\mu$) and quadrupole-dipole ($\nu\text{-}\mu$) couplings. By employing a complete set of basis functions for rotational states, effective Hamiltonians are derived for basis states corresponding to various relative orientations of the dimer pairs. Analysis of the resulting Hamiltonian matrix elements reveals that basis functions with specific symmetries yield significantly larger interaction dipole moments than others. Consequently, these Hamiltonians facilitate a precise calculation of the IDMs for any given pair of orientations. Furthermore, the study confirms that the absolute value of the total interaction dipole moment remains invariant regardless of the dimer's overall spatial rotation.

The prevailing lack of visibility into decision-making processes hinders organizational efficiency, often resulting in budget inaccuracies and delayed shipments. This study introduces a decision traceability framework designed to enhance operational transparency and resolve these issues. By utilizing a time-event model, we capture the specific timing and sequencing of decisions, which effectively represents both hierarchical and parallel decision structures. We have developed a dedicated modeling language to describe these scenarios and a corresponding analysis tool that generates time-event models from decision logs. This capability enables a detailed reconstruction of decision paths and the quantification of associated lead times. Ultimately, this approach offers a robust foundation for diagnosing current decision-making processes and providing a necessary step toward real-time operational management.

Resiliency is a critical aspect of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), involving a system's capacity to recover from unexpected events while maintaining essential functions. While the field has seen extensive research into modeling CPS for system analysis, there remains a scarcity of work specifically modeling the resiliency of these integrated systems. This paper introduces the Resilient Petri Net (PRWN), an extension of the traditional Petri net framework designed to capture the dynamic behaviors of resilient CPSs. We outline the necessary conditions for maintaining CPS resiliency and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PRWN approach through the case study of a water treatment plant.

This review offers a concise overview of dark matter research, addressing the fundamental questions of what constitutes it and its interaction with ordinary matter. While general audiences often associate dark matter with WIMPs, axions, or sterile neutrinos, the underlying physics remains poorly understood, leading to a lack of definitive detection evidence. This uncertainty has prompted a shift in focus toward indirect detection, particularly through astrophysical signals. This chapter examines recent progress in indirect dark matter searches, with particular attention to signals generated by superheavy neutral stable particles (HNSPs) that may be produced via mechanisms such as black hole evaporation.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) represent a prominent category of probabilistic models, formally expressed as Bayesian networks where each node corresponds to a discrete Markov chain. Typically, these models are constructed using the method of maximum likelihood estimation via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. However, the convergence of the MCMC process can be significantly hindered by the presence of numerous local optima. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework for modeling complex temporal dependencies. This approach involves decomposing a Hidden Markov model into multiple simpler submodels, each characterized by a single transition. We achieve this decomposition by introducing a latent variable that partitions the original set of hidden states. Consequently, the resulting modular structure facilitates the application of the EM algorithm to the parameters of these submodels, while the augmented data created by the splitting of hidden states allows for the utilization of standard MCMC techniques on the primary mixture model.

This work addresses the challenge of modeling turbulent flows using the framework of stochastic advection, where known velocity fields are treated as Brownian motions defined on compact manifolds. In such scenarios, particle trajectories correspond to random paths (Brownian motions) on the associated group of vector fields. We demonstrate that the law governing these pullback dynamics constitutes a solution to a specific partial differential equation (DE) on the group of vector fields. Furthermore, we provide practical algorithms for numerically approximating these pullback measures, effectively resolving the forward propagators of a backward Kolmogorov equation. Finally, our discussion outlines strategies for inverting this process to approximate a time-dependent, backward Kolmogorov equation, utilizing these tools to estimate pullback measures.

This work outlines a technique to fit and choose folding models for nuclear elastic scattering that surpasses previous methods. By employing an ensemble of initial optical potentials generated via a bootstrap approach, we perform a simultaneous fit to the scattering data using these ensembles across various existing folding models. This strategy mitigates the biases inherent in relying on a single starting point and offers a more reliable evaluation of each model's viability. In applications to the $^{6}$Li+$^{208}$Pb elastic scattering system, our results indicate that the density-dependent local energy-dependent model performs best among the alternatives tested.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of electromagnetic radiation confined within a one-dimensional cavity of thickness $2L$. By deriving expressions for energy density and pressure, we examine how these quantities vary with temperature and the ratio of thermal wavelength to the system size. At low temperatures where $k_BT \lesssim \hbar c/L$, the radiation behaves similarly to a dilute gas of photons, but as the system approaches thermal equilibrium in the bulk limit of $LR/\hbar \to 0$, pressure and energy density diverge from standard predictions. In this regime, the bulk limit remains consistent with blackbody thermodynamics only when the zero-temperature Casimir force is subtracted. We attribute this anomaly to the presence of a high-frequency cutoff imposed by the slab's finite thickness, which ultimately aligns our findings with recent analyses of bulk blackbody radiation near perfect mirrors.

Hiding users' trajectories is essential for protecting the privacy of location-based services, particularly when multiple positions are exposed in rapid succession. Existing research primarily addresses trajectory inference by analyzing user movement patterns, yet this approach fails to provide robust privacy because those patterns can be easily reversed to reveal identities. This study instead examines the problem through the lens of social relationships, proposing a new framework for anonymizing user paths. The goal is to ensure that at least a minimum number of relationships remain obscured from potential attackers, thereby preventing pattern-based de-anonymization. The authors introduce the "Minimum Trajectory Perturbation" (MinTP) algorithm, which optimizes trajectory modification to maximize similarity with the original route while satisfying social relationship constraints. Experimental results on a real-world dataset demonstrate that MinTP successfully provides strong privacy guarantees with only slight deviations from actual movements. Furthermore, the study confirms that MinTP can be effectively extended to protect other forms of sensitive relational data.

Autonomous driving heavily relies on 3D point cloud–based place recognition, especially in areas where GPS is unreliable. While existing methods predominantly utilize global descriptors, they often struggle with significant rotations, scale variations, and low-texture point clouds. To address these challenges, we introduce a new approach that integrates local and global descriptors for robust recognition. Specifically, we employ a 3D-CNN to generate global descriptors from 3D voxel grids constructed from point clouds. For local descriptors, we employ a Siamese network trained on local structures extracted via random sample consensus (RCS) to ensure accurate point-to-plane registration. Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid framework effectively handles large rotational changes, scaling variations, and scenarios involving low texture in point cloud data.
